speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Ruth Anderson Kellberg has lived her entire life on Burnt Ridge near Troy. She reads a written statement on this tape about early life on the ridge and early religious services. In addition, she recalls the early morning Christmas service, Luther League, Peter Carlson, party games, hoeing beans, and shopping in Moscow.

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Pioneer men and women arrived and settled in this area in 1883 and 1884. Among them was Carl Anderson, who arrived from Ashtabula, Ohio in 1884 after working at that place for three years after he arrived in Sweden. Carl took up a homestead on what is now Burnt Ridge. He and two other bachelors shared the same cabin. Land had to be cleared, as everywhere you looked there was brush. Great were the privations of these early settlers. Their earnings were very meager, working at sawmills which were located some distance away. One year the sawmill company went broke and the men did not receive one penny for their hard labor all through that year. As their only conveyance was their own two feet, they were only able to come home on weekends. Part of these weekends were spent in carrying water from the stream, clear down at the railroad track. One of these pioneers, Andrew Westberg, who brought his wife with him from Sweden, saw a bear one day. He did not dare tell his wife about this, for fear she could become frightened, being left alone all week. When he arrived home that weekend, he found his wife's headscarf as he was crossing the little stream close by. He then feared the worst had happened. His fears were ungrounded, however, as he found his wife well and happy. The nearest place where these pioneers could get their supplies was at Moscow. They had to walk all this distance until they had earned enough to buy a team of horses and a lumber wagon. It was not easy carrying a sack of flour on their back and any other groceries which were needed. One time Anderson was trudging along the road, tired and hungry, when he noticed a biscuit on top of the snow along the roadside. He picked it up, ate it, and felt good from it. He concluded a higher power had seen that it was placed there just for a hungry man. Another family arrived in 1906. This party was instrumental in getting the telephone into the homes of these settlers. One person he could not persuade to get a telephone was his brother-in-law. One day a horse fell into the well at the brother-in-law's place. Kellberg asked him if he didn't wish he had a telephone so he could call for help. Well, a telephone was soon installed. Anderson's mother arrived from Sweden at the age of 70, about the year of 1888. Not being able to cope with the language, she was taken clear over to the state of Utah, where her trunk was stolen, with the few belongings she had. She was very tired when she arrived at the cabin, having to ride from Moscow in the number wagon. Anderson's sister, Sophie Anderson, arrived from Ohio in 1894 to keep house for her brother. A few years later the town of Helmer, later called Troy, came into being. No gravel. Imagine the horses plodding knee deep in this mire of mud through Main Street. What a buggy ride through town. These early immigrants walked clear to the Linville country to worship at the Cordelia Chapel. Their future hope lay in organizing a church where they could worship God. Pastor Peter Carlson came to bring God's word to these pioneer settlers. As he started out from Moscow on foot, Anderson would meet him with his horses and number wagon. Pastor Carlson ate many a meal at the home of these bachelors. Pastor Carlson conducted worship services in the various homes. And in December 1886, a group of these pioneers met and organized the Lutheran church with 17 charter members.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: I want to have you tell me the names of the other two men who came out with your father. Weren't they both Johnsons?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Olaf Johnson and August Johnson.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Was August and...

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: They were not related.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Now, did they know each other before?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: They knew each other from Sweden.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Did your father ever talk about his life in Ashtabula, Ohio?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: My uncle.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Your uncle, huh?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Well, some. He worked very hard there on the... at the docks hauling coal in wheelbarrows.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Did your uncle ever talk about that wet harvest in 93 or any particular bad times that they had?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: I don't remember too much about it, but he did mention the hard times they had at that time. They were very hard.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Had things changed a lot by the time you were born and remember?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Oh, I think so. It was quite a depression during those years. I don't know just how long they lasted. I don't remember. I was only four when my grandmother passed away, but I remember a few things about her.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: What do you remember?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Well, I remember when we moved into this house. We lived in sort of a shack before down in the orchard. My brother and my aunt and uncle were carrying the stove, moving the stove in. I and grandmother came behind them with her cane, and I was carrying the coffee pot. Then when we came into the house, my uncle said, Now we must have some coffee.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: So that was what you did. There was something else I remembered, which was the cross that your mother made when Peter Carlson passed away.

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: My aunt, Sophie Anderson. She made a cross out of tin cans and soldered it so it held water, and then she filled it with pansies. It was really beautiful, but it was quite heavy. She had sand in there, too, so that they'd stay in.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Were you young when you passed away?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Yes, I was quite young. I don't know just how old. I don't know. Probably seven, eight years old. I don't know. I really don't know.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: When you were young, were there things that you did around the house, chores that you had to do?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Oh, yes. When I got old enough, I milked cows, took care of the chickens, helped my aunt clean the flowerbed. She had raised a lot of pansies and other flowers.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: When you were at home, you always spoke Swedish, didn't you?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: We always spoke Swedish. My uncle couldn't manage the American language pretty well, but my aunt was not very good at it, so we always spoke Swedish. When I started school, I didn't know much about the English language. I even spoke Swedish to the teacher when he asked me questions.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: What did he think of that?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Oh, he didn't say anything.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Were there other children that didn't know English when you went to school?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: I don't remember. I don't think so.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Was it hard to learn?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: No, I think it came quite easily. Okay.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Do you know anything about the tuberculosis that was on the ridge here? The children that died?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: No, not much. No.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: It didn't affect you at all?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: My husband had two sisters that died from it.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: What kind of things when you were young did you do for fun?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Well, we had literary societies at the schoolhouse, and there were debates carried on about different things. And we had Young People's Society, Luther League, we called it from the church, and we met in the various homes in the evenings during the summer. After the programs, we'd play games outside on the lawn. We'd have a lot of fun.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Was that religious at all?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: The programs were.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Did you take part in those programs?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Yes.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: What did you ever do there?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: I don't remember much about that. I think we mainly spoke. I don't remember much about the programs.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Do you remember any of the games that you played afterwards?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Oh, we played a lot of Swedish games and sang to them. Party games, we called them.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Do you remember any of them?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Only in Swedish.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Could you sing them to me in Swedish? And then tell me afterwards what they were about?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Well, I know one in English. We're sailing east, we're sailing west, we're sailing over the ocean. You sailor boy, if you want a good wife, you better be quick in your motion.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: There were movements that went with that, weren't there?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Yes.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Do you remember any of the Swedish ones?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Oh, I don't know. Not so good. It's been quite a while.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: When did they stop doing those party games?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Oh, that was when we grew up. In our later teens, I guess.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Did the church have other activities that you went to? Or anything?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Well, I don't remember too much. We had church services in the morning, in the Sundays.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Were those in Swedish when you were young?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Yes… there wasn't near as much activities in the church then as it is now.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Did most of the people on the ridge belong to the church?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Yes, most of them did.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Did they all go into town together?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Well, each in their own rigs.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Did you go to families for dinner afterwards?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Yes, we did that a whole lot more then than we do now. It seems that the cars have taken over now and you go farther, longer distance. Then we stayed close by more so.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Do you remember much about school? Any days when you went there?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Well, we went to school in a one-room schoolhouse. All eight grades, one teacher. At one time we were 44 pupils. Quite a bunch for one teacher to take care of.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Would she have trouble? Would the teacher have trouble?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Sometimes. Some of the boys did sometimes.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Did you go through the eighth grade?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: I finished the eighth grade up here, yeah.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: What did you do after that?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Well, that's all the schooling I had because we didn't have any conveyance to go to Troy, to high school at that time.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: I meant more what you, you know, after you left school what you did?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Well, then I worked on the farm after all. We raised beans a lot at that time and there was a lot of beans hoeing around for different neighbors.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: You'd hoe for other neighbors?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Yes… all day long. Didn't mind the sun as much then as now… that's hard work… well, yes.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: What did you do?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Well, they were planted in rows so we had to hoe out the weeds. And then in the fall when they were ripe we bunched them. When they were dry they'd come along and pick them up and put them in stacks. After a while, thrash them.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: What else did you grow around here? What else did your uncle grow?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Wheat and oats and barley.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: He had an orchard too, right?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Yes. He had a lot of fruit trees. Apples and mainly prunes. We had a large prune orchard.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Do you remember much about that? Did you pick prunes?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Well, I was really too little to pick much at that time. The main thing was for grandma to keep me in the house so I wouldn't go down there and bother them when they were picking prunes.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: When did they stop that orchard? Did they chop it down?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: They pulled out the trees. After a while, I don't know, just when.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Were there any other people on Burt Ridge when your uncle came here? Or were those three men pretty much the first settlers out here?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Well, I think the Westburg family came. Him and his wife came earlier. And there were probably a few others that didn't come from Sweden. Maybe two or three families.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Do you know what made your uncle leave Sweden?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Well, I don't know exactly but I think they had a hard time of it in Sweden. Everybody went to America. I guess it was just sort of a fever that everybody went here. I thought this would be a better country, I guess.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: How long was he in Ashtabula?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Three years. From 1881 to 1884.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Did you go to Moscow much when you were young?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Once a year we went there to do a lot of shopping. Usually in the fall of the year on a team of horses in Surrey. We didn't make those trips very often because that would take quite a while, you know. My uncle brought hay along for the horses to eat in the feed stable. And we'd do our shopping at the Williamson store. And he was real tickled that we came, you know. That was a far distance to come. And he ran a cafeteria there so he'd always give us a good free dinner. So that was quite a treat. Yeah.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Once a year… gosh… did you ever... you could get your whole... what you needed for the whole year? Just one?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Well, maybe. This was mainly clothing.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Did you get into Troy much?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Well, we went in Troy every week, of course.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: But you didn't go into shop or anything much?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Get groceries and things.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Did you know your husband for a long time before you got married?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Oh yes, we grew up together here on the same ridge. Went to school together.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Were you very old when you were married?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: I was 26… did your husband...

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: did he stay at home before he married you?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Yes, he was at home working on his father's farm. They were a large family so there was a lot of work to do.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Were you close friends for a long time before you got married?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Yes.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Did you work out at all?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: No, I didn't… i had plenty of work to do right here.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: I know you've told me a lot more than you're telling me now. You gave me short answers. But I don't have any more questions. But I know that there's more that you can say about your life than you were young. Are there any more things that your uncle told you that you remember?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: No, I don't remember too much. I often wished I'd found out more from him. But I was young then, you know, and I didn't think of those things. But I wish I had.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Was it many, many years that they got their water from the creek and that they hauled it up here?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Well, I suppose they dug a cistern as soon as they could. When they had the means of getting it hauled from town. I don't know just how long it was.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Did they have the early Christmas service?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Yes, we did… and we enjoyed that so much. 5:30 on Christmas morning. And we'd ride to town in the sled and drawn by horses, sleigh bells. That was beautiful. Cold, you know. We didn't mind that. It was a lot of fun. And in the early morning my aunt would get up and have a candle lit in each window, upstairs and downstairs. And that was my job to watch those candles run up and down the steps to see that everything was okay. And that was a lot of fun. When we went to church we blew them out, of course. It was dark on our way to church and when we came out it was daylight.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: How was that fun? Was everyone really happy?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Yes, yes… and it was traditional. And we missed it after it was gone.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Why did they do away with that?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Well, I think it was mainly because the people in town didn't want to get up that early in the morning. So now we have it at 11 o 'clock Christmas Eve in the evening. It was easier for you to get up at 5:30 than to stay up until 11 in the afternoon. Well, I didn't mind it one bit.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Did you get presents for Christmas too?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Yes, we did. We gave our presents on Christmas Eve… well, that's...

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: The only thing is, do you remember Peter Carlson at all? Did you know him?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: I don't think I remember him. Only by pictures. No, I don't. That was really before my time.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Would he come out to Troy and give fun?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Yes, he did.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Was there another pastor? Who was the early pastors in Troy?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Well, they came from Moscow because the church there was organized earlier than Troy. So there was N .J .W. Nelson, George Anderson, and Reverend Beckman. He was the first one, really.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Were they all good men?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Yes, oh yes.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Did they stay around here?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: No, they just came down. You could go on the train at that time. Probably had... I don't know when the cars came in, really. Not for the early ones, no. Then when our church was organized in church, and we had a regular pastor later on, that is.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: When was that about?

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: That's when they organized it? What were you going to say?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: Later on, the pastors would come out to the schoolhouses in the country on Sunday afternoons and preach.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Was that for the school children?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: No.

speaker: Laura Schrager
words: Or just for those people?

speaker: Ruth Anderson Kellberg
words: It was a little harder to get into town then when we had to ride on horses, I guess.
